draft.title: Algorithms and pseudocode
card: An algorithm is a list of steps that solves a problem and always ends. Pseudocode writes those steps in plain, code-like words, so any person can follow them.
Sequence
steps run one after another, in order. Changing the order can change the result.
Decision
an if-then step runs only when a condition is true. Example: if n > 10 then set n to 10.
Loop
a set of steps repeats. Example: set total to 0, then for each i from 1 to 3, set total to total + i. The steps run 3 times, so total becomes 1, then 3, then 6.
draft.remember: Sequence gives the order, decisions choose, loops repeat.

a.q: An algorithm sets n to 4, then runs: if n > 10 then set n to 10. Then it sets n to n + 2. What is the final value of n?
a.why: n is 4, so n > 10 is false and the if-then step is skipped. Then n + 2 = 6. The answer 12 comes from running the if-then step as if it were true, which would make n 10 and then 12.
a.clue: Check whether the condition is true before running the step.

b.q: An algorithm sets total to 0. Then for each i from 1 to 4, it sets total to total + 2 × i. What is the final value of total?
b.why: The loop adds 2, 4, 6 and 8, and 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20. Check: 2 × (1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 2 × 10 = 20. The answer 10 forgets the 2 ×, and 8 gives only the last pass.
b.clue: List what is added on each pass of the loop, then add them up.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers are correct: n stays 4 because the condition is false, then becomes 6; the loop adds 2, 4, 6 and 8 to give 20.

b.q: An algorithm sets total to 0. Then for each \(i\) from 1 to 4, it sets total to \(\text{total} + 2 \times i\). What is the final value of total?
b.why: The loop adds 2, 4, 6 and 8, and \(2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20\). Check: \(2 \times (1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 2 \times 10 = 20\). The answer 10 forgets the \(2 \times\), and 8 gives only the last pass.
b.clue: List what is added on each pass of the loop, then add them up.
